claims.claim: The widower Joel Thompson's verdict on the machine-summarised obituary of his wife, in his own words to WIRED, was that it read as a child's work.
claims.source: Joel Thompson, quoted by Ben Weiss, WIRED, 26 Dec 2021
claims.quote: It looks like a fourth grader did it

claims.claim: Oswald, relaying LiveScience's report of OpenAI research, states that two of OpenAI's most advanced models hallucinated 33% and 48% of the time.
claims.source: Anjelica Oswald, Vita Brevis, relaying Roland Moore-Colyer, LiveScience, 21 June 2025
claims.quote: hallucinated” 33% and 48% of the time

claims.claim: CelebrateAlly's founder says she routes creative obituary writing to OpenAI's GPT4 Turbo and more logical messages to Anthropic's Claude.
claims.source: Sonali George of CelebrateAlly, reported by Drew Harwell, The Washington Post, 3 Aug 2025
claims.quote: OpenAI’s GPT4 Turbo

claims.claim: In the same relayed test the tool wrote that the man's strength was not merely physical prowess but an inner fortitude.
claims.source: a CelebrateAlly output quoted by Frank Landymore, Futurism, 4 Aug 2025, relaying the Washington Post's test
claims.quote: not merely physical prowess, but an inner fortitude

claims.claim: Futurism characterises the tool's habit as making up details and slathering them in sententious, flowery language.
claims.source: Frank Landymore, Futurism, 4 Aug 2025
claims.quote: slathering them in sententious, flowery language

claims.claim: A reader's post quoted by Futurism states that AI should not be writing obituaries.
claims.source: an unnamed reader post quoted by Victor Tangermann, Futurism, 14 Sep 2023
claims.quote: AI should not be writing obituaries

claims.claim: Microsoft's Jeff Jones said of MSN's earlier incoherent Ottawa travel guide that it was not produced by a large language model or AI system.
claims.source: Jeff Jones, senior director at Microsoft, quoted to The Verge and relayed by Victor Tangermann, Futurism, 14 Sep 2023
claims.quote: not a large language model or AI system

claims.claim: In Meister and colleagues' human evaluation the human reference string was ranked first in 47 percent of cases and tied for first in a further 16 percent.
claims.source: Clara Meister, Gian Wiher, Tiago Pimentel and Ryan Cotterell, 'On the probability-quality paradox in language generation', ACL 2022 (arXiv v1, 31 Mar 2022)
claims.quote: was ranked first in 47% of cases

claims.claim: Welleck and colleagues state that top-k and nucleus sampling do not address the underlying problem that the model's token-level probabilities are poor.
claims.source: Sean Welleck, Ilia Kulikov, Stephen Roller, Emily Dinan, Kyunghyun Cho and Jason Weston, 'Neural Text Generation with Unlikelihood Training', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 26 Sep 2019)
claims.quote: they do not address the fact that the token-level probabilities predicted

claims.claim: Welleck and colleagues measured that greedy decoding from their Transformer language model produced 43 percent repeated n-grams against 0.5 percent for human text on the same prefixes.
claims.source: Sean Welleck, Ilia Kulikov, Stephen Roller, Emily Dinan, Kyunghyun Cho and Jason Weston, 'Neural Text Generation with Unlikelihood Training', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 26 Sep 2019)
claims.quote: greedy decoding (43%) far exceeds that of humans

claims.claim: Welleck and colleagues measured that greedy next-token predictions on held-out Wikitext-103 used roughly 40 percent fewer unique tokens than the ground truth, 11.6 thousand against 18.9 thousand.
claims.source: Sean Welleck, Ilia Kulikov, Stephen Roller, Emily Dinan, Kyunghyun Cho and Jason Weston, 'Neural Text Generation with Unlikelihood Training', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 26 Sep 2019)
claims.quote: roughly 40% fewer unique tokens than the ground-truth tokens

claims.claim: Welleck and colleagues connect the model's under-use of rare words to human judgments of dullness, on the ground that rare words add engaging specificity.
claims.source: Sean Welleck, Ilia Kulikov, Stephen Roller, Emily Dinan, Kyunghyun Cho and Jason Weston, 'Neural Text Generation with Unlikelihood Training', ICLR 2020 (arXiv v2, 26 Sep 2019)
claims.quote: rare words can add engaging specificity

claims.claim: Kirk and colleagues measured that RLHF significantly reduces output diversity relative to supervised fine-tuning across a range of diversity measures.
claims.source: Robert Kirk, Ishita Mediratta, Christoforos Nalmpantis, Jelena Luketina, Eric Hambro, Edward Grefenstette and Roberta Raileanu, 'Understanding the Effects of RLHF on LLM Generalisation and Diversity', ICLR 2024 (arXiv v3, 19 Feb 2024)
claims.quote: RLHF significantly reduces output diversity compared to

claims.claim: Kirk and colleagues found that RLHF-tuned models produce less diverse text even across different inputs, so they tend to write similarly whatever they are asked.
claims.source: Robert Kirk, Ishita Mediratta, Christoforos Nalmpantis, Jelena Luketina, Eric Hambro, Edward Grefenstette and Roberta Raileanu, 'Understanding the Effects of RLHF on LLM Generalisation and Diversity', ICLR 2024 (arXiv v3, 19 Feb 2024)
claims.quote: tend to produce more similar text regardless of the input

claims.claim: All 35 passages the reporters drew from the AI-suspected France guidebook scored 100 on Originality.ai's AI detector.
claims.source: Seth Kugel and Stephen Hiltner, The New York Times, 5 August 2023
claims.quote: All 35 passages scored a perfect 100

claims.claim: Of 190 paragraphs the reporters tested from 64 further comparably formatted guidebooks, 166 scored 100 and only 12 scored under 75.
claims.source: Seth Kugel and Stephen Hiltner, The New York Times, 5 August 2023
claims.quote: 166 scored 100, and only 12 scored under 75

claims.claim: Passages from the human travel brands Rick Steves, Fodor's, Frommer's and Lonely Planet scored nearly all under 10 on the same detector, the control against which the guidebook scores were read.
claims.source: Seth Kugel and Stephen Hiltner, The New York Times, 5 August 2023
claims.quote: nearly all under 10

claims.claim: Originality.ai claimed the detector version used mistakes human text for AI on just under 1.6 percent of tests.
claims.source: Originality.ai's claim as reported by The New York Times, 5 August 2023
claims.quote: just under 1.6 percent of tests

claims.claim: The reader who bought the AI-suspected France guidebook was disappointed by its vague descriptions, in the reporters' paraphrase of her.
claims.source: Amy Kolsky, paraphrased by Seth Kugel and Stephen Hiltner, The New York Times, 5 August 2023
claims.quote: vague descriptions, repetitive text and lack of itineraries

claims.claim: The same reader found the guidebook's text repetitive, in the reporters' paraphrase of her.
claims.source: Amy Kolsky, paraphrased by Seth Kugel and Stephen Hiltner, The New York Times, 5 August 2023
claims.quote: vague descriptions, repetitive text and lack of itineraries

claims.claim: The reader's own account of the guidebook was that it read as though facts had been copied off the internet and pasted in.
claims.source: Amy Kolsky quoted in The New York Times, 5 August 2023
claims.quote: copied a whole bunch of information from Wikipedia and just pasted

claims.claim: More than ten guidebooks published under one author name shared a cookie-cutter design and similar promotional language, the reporters found.
claims.source: Seth Kugel and Stephen Hiltner, The New York Times, 5 August 2023
claims.quote: same cookie-cutter design and use similar promotional language

claims.claim: Frommer's editorial director Pauline Frommer characterised the imitation guidebooks as sweeping the internet and putting random crap down.
claims.source: Pauline Frommer quoted in The New York Times, 5 August 2023
claims.quote: sweep the internet and put random crap down

claims.claim: Darby Rollins, founder of a company that helps businesses use generative AI, judged the guidebooks very basic.
claims.source: Darby Rollins quoted in The New York Times, 5 August 2023
claims.quote: very basic

claims.claim: The one Wikivoyage user known to have posted AI-generated discussion comments was disruptive mostly through flowery language, according to the editor who dealt with it.
claims.source: User:LPfi, Wikivoyage talk:AI guidelines, 16 May 2026
claims.quote: highly disruptive, mostly by using flowery language

claims.claim: The oddly specific cocktail ChatGPT ordered the writer to request, which he expected to be fabricated, turned out to exist.
claims.source: Thom Brown, Intrepid Times, 2 January 2026
claims.quote: It’s real,” I beam

claims.claim: The writer's summary judgement is that he prefers a human-written guide to the slop AI puts between practical advice.
claims.source: Thom Brown, Intrepid Times, 2 January 2026
claims.quote: the sprinkles of slop that AI tends to vomit between practical

claims.claim: The same policy discloses that AI does write the reader-facing quick-summary blocks at the top of certain destination articles, condensing human reporting within editorially designed templates.
claims.source: Lonely Planet, Editorial Policy on AI (vendor page, fetched 6 September 2026)
claims.quote: Quick-summary blocks at the top of certain destination articles

claims.claim: Wikipedia's editor-maintained catalogue of AI tells states that even when prompted to use an encyclopedic style, LLM output will often tend toward advertisement-like writing or the prose of a travel guide.
claims.source: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing (WikiProject AI Cleanup advice page), revision fetched 6 September 2026
claims.quote: their output will often tend toward advertisement-like writing, or like the prose of a travel guide

claims.claim: The same page states that LLMs tend to over-use the same set of promotional phrases no matter what the topic.
claims.source: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, revision fetched 6 September 2026
claims.quote: LLMs tend to over-use the same set of promotional phrases no matter what the topic

claims.claim: An April 2024 revision to the Wikipedia article on Korattur closed with the formula that despite its industrial and residential prosperity, Korattur faces challenges.
claims.source: AI-generated Wikipedia text from an April 2024 revision to Korattur, quoted as an example in Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing
claims.quote: Despite its industrial and residential prosperity, Korattur faces challenges

claims.claim: The same page states that older LLMs such as GPT-4 output more blatantly positive text than newer ones, which are more subtly positive and tend to avoid obviously superlative statements.
claims.source: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, revision fetched 6 September 2026, citing Sussman and Carter
claims.quote: more subtly positive and tend to avoid obviously superlative statements

claims.claim: The same page states that the words LLMs overuse have changed over time.
claims.source: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, revision fetched 6 September 2026
claims.quote: The words that LLMs overuse have changed over time

claims.claim: The same page reports that the word delve was famously overused by ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024.
claims.source: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, revision fetched 6 September 2026, citing Merrill, Chen and Kumer in The Washington Post and Geng and Trotta
claims.quote: was famously overused by ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024

claims.claim: The same page states that AI linguistic patterns occur consistently regardless of subject matter, which often gives AI-generated text an identifiable voice.
claims.source: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, revision fetched 6 September 2026
claims.quote: which often gives AI-generated text an identifiable "voice"

claims.claim: The English Wikipedia AI-cleanup advice page groups the overused-word tells by model era, assigning 'delve', 'tapestry', 'testament', 'meticulous' and 'pivotal' to a 2023 to mid-2024 GPT-4 era.
claims.source: English Wikipedia advice page 'Signs of AI writing' (WikiProject AI Cleanup), section 'High density of AI vocabulary words'

claims.claim: The same page records that 'delve' became less frequent later in 2024 and then dropped off sharply in 2025.
claims.source: English Wikipedia advice page 'Signs of AI writing', section 'High density of AI vocabulary words'
claims.quote: became less frequent later in 2024, then dropped off sharply in 2025

claims.claim: The page asserts that the AI-vocabulary words are ubiquitous in LLM-built encyclopedias such as Grokipedia as well as in AI-generated Wikipedia text.
claims.source: English Wikipedia advice page 'Signs of AI writing', section 'High density of AI vocabulary words'
claims.quote: words are also ubiquitous in LLM-based encyclopedias

claims.claim: A September 2026 maintenance banner on the em dash section proposes moving it to historical indicators because the sign seems to be less common in current LLM output.
claims.source: English Wikipedia advice page 'Signs of AI writing', banner on section 'Overuse of em dashes'
claims.quote: it seems to be less common in current LLM output

claims.claim: The page asserts that LLMs overuse the rule of three, from 'adjective, adjective, adjective' to 'short phrase, short phrase, and short phrase'.
claims.source: English Wikipedia advice page 'Signs of AI writing', section 'Rule of three'
claims.quote: LLMs overuse the rule of three

claims.claim: The page states that the not-just-X-but-Y parallelism is common among human writers yet is stereotypically treated as an AI sign.
claims.source: English Wikipedia advice page 'Signs of AI writing', section 'Negative parallelisms'
claims.quote: it is stereotypically an "AI sign."

claims.claim: The page states that LLM writing puffs up the importance of the subject by adding statements about how arbitrary aspects of the topic contribute to a broader topic.
claims.source: English Wikipedia advice page 'Signs of AI writing', section 'Undue emphasis on significance, legacy, and broader trends'
claims.quote: puffs up the importance of the subject matter

claims.claim: The page tells editors that humans are notoriously bad at distinguishing human from LLM-generated text.
claims.source: English Wikipedia advice page 'Signs of AI writing', section 'Your detection ability'
claims.quote: Humans are notoriously bad at distinguishing human and LLM-generated text

claims.claim: The page warns that a word being overused by AI does not imply its synonyms are also overused.
claims.source: English Wikipedia advice page 'Signs of AI writing', section 'High density of AI vocabulary words'
claims.quote: a word being overused by AI does

claims.claim: Yasseri measured that Grokipedia entries are systematically longer than their matched Wikipedia counterparts across 17,790 article pairs.
claims.source: Taha Yasseri, 'How Similar Are Grokipedia and Wikipedia?', 2025
claims.quote: Grokipedia entries are systematically longer than their Wikipedia counterparts

claims.claim: In the same study Grokipedia articles average 7,662 words against 6,280 on Wikipedia.
claims.source: Taha Yasseri, 2025, Table 1 (all pairs)
claims.quote: Grokipedia articles average 7,662 words versus 6,280 on Wikipedia

claims.claim: In the same test Alexander found the model renamed its own just-established ship detail one line later, which he calls forgetting what it had just said.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, comment on his own post, The Alexandrian
claims.quote: It immediately forgot what it just said.

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch, who reviews commercial adventures and setting books full time, says he cannot recognise AI-written products that his readers spot easily.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, comment on his own review, tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: I just don’t understand how people can recognize it so easily.

claims.claim: A commenter on that review argues a first glance will not reveal machine-generated text because imitating conventional writing well enough to pass is what LLMs are for.
claims.source: commenter 'DP', tenfootpole.org comment thread
claims.quote: to imitate conventional writing enough to pass for man-made

claims.claim: A commenter argues that the recognisable 'ChatGPT Voice' is deliberately built into that product and is not common to all LLMs, so readers who know only ChatGPT overestimate their ability to detect generated text.
claims.source: commenter 'LettuceBeReal', tenfootpole.org comment thread
claims.quote: the “ChatGPT Voice” that OpenAI purposefully bakes into it

claims.claim: A commenter demonstrating that the reviewed setting book was human-written pasted one of its ungrammatical setting sentences into ChatGPT, and the returned rewrite fixed the grammar and regularised the construction.
claims.source: commenter 'Blakely', tenfootpole.org comment thread, quoting ChatGPT output
claims.quote: This version tightens the flow

claims.claim: Hargrave says that after prompting several options for Wingspan card ideas, not one gave her an actionable idea.
claims.source: Elizabeth Hargrave to BoardGameWire, quoted by Mike Didymus-True, Rascal News
claims.quote: not one of them has given me an actionable idea

claims.claim: A commenter who had tested AI adventure generation himself says the reviewed text matches the way the model replies, naming its hedging vocabulary as the tell.
claims.source: commenter 'AB Andy', tenfootpole.org comment thread
claims.quote: With maybe, perhaps, could be.

claims.claim: A commenter who had previously argued that readers over-accuse adventures of being LLM-written says this product's preview is absolutely machine-written with minimal editing.
claims.source: commenter 'Quentin', tenfootpole.org comment thread
claims.quote: it is absolutely written by a machine with minimal editing

claims.claim: A commenter argues no AI-detection technology is needed for this material because filtering for quality already excludes it.
claims.source: anonymous commenter, tenfootpole.org comment thread
claims.quote: simply filtering for quality will also exclude it

claims.claim: A commenter judges that an adventure widely suspected of being machine-written does not read like an LLM, and says people wildly overestimate LLMs.
claims.source: commenter 'Quentin', tenfootpole.org comment thread on 'The Snake Temple Ruins'
claims.quote: It doesn’t read like an LLM.

claims.claim: The adventure's author states in the comments that he wrote it without any AI help, having used AI only on the artwork.
claims.source: Olly Tyler, author, in the tenfootpole.org comment thread
claims.quote: I wrote this adventure without any AI help.

claims.claim: That guide cites an October 2024 revision of the article on Kumba, Cameroon, in which road networks are said to have helped the town solidify its role as a regional hub, as an instance of the pattern.
claims.source: WikiProject AI Cleanup, 'Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing', quoting the Kumba, Cameroon article
claims.quote: solidify its role as a regional hub

claims.claim: The guide states that AI chatbots insert superficial analysis of information, often about its significance, recognition or impact.
claims.source: WikiProject AI Cleanup, 'Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing'
claims.quote: AI chatbots tend to insert superficial analysis of information

claims.claim: The guide states that many studies have found LLMs overuse a specific set of words, and lists them as words to watch.
claims.source: WikiProject AI Cleanup, 'Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing'
claims.quote: Many studies have demonstrated that LLMs overuse specific words.

claims.claim: The guide notes that while most studies of these overused words analysed scientific abstracts or fiction, the same words are ubiquitous in LLM-based encyclopedias.
claims.source: WikiProject AI Cleanup, 'Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing'
claims.quote: words are also ubiquitous in LLM-based encyclopedias, such as

claims.claim: The guide reports that these words began appearing far more frequently in text produced after 2022, when LLM chatbots became widely accessible.
claims.source: WikiProject AI Cleanup, 'Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing'
claims.quote: These words started appearing far more frequently in text produced after 2022

claims.claim: The guide reports a July 2026 study finding that among contemporary models only Claude used em dashes more than professional writers, while ChatGPT used them less.
claims.source: WikiProject AI Cleanup, 'Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing', citing a July 2026 study
claims.quote: only Claude used em dashes more than professional writers

claims.claim: The guide warns that not all text showing these indicators is AI-generated, since the models were trained on human writing and many of the elements occur in editorials, blogs and fan fiction.
claims.source: WikiProject AI Cleanup, 'Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing'
claims.quote: Not all text featuring these indicators is AI-generated
